Body: I would look around at job listings for your area and concentrate on what employers are looking for. I’m self-employed and my clients are either C# or Java based so I bounce between them. If you have spare time, I would learn SQL over the COBOL.
You nailed it, university is easy compared to real work. And if he can't handle university, then what are we even talking about

Learn one language at a time. Do projects with it. Find a job with it. And then start the next one.

If you already learn Java at school, it is a genuine mistake starting learning C# and COBOL in parallel. It doesn’t have any sense, really.

What could have a sense next to Java:

- Learning Kotlin to learn “a better Java”

- Learning Clojure to learn a functional language

And that’s it.
I’d say Java,JavaScript, and Python. Get a senior level in JavaScript and Java and you’ll be unstoppable.

i think java is used for backend development, so if you are comfortable in that language it will be easier for you. and also i think java and spring are pretty popular, i feel like c# would be useful if you want to get into gamedev or into .NET. i also find a lot of things interesting, but it's better to just focus on one thing at a time, otherwise you are going to get overwhelmed.
[It's never too late to get into tech](https://www.trevorlasn.com/blog/ageism-in-tech). Seriously.

"Jack of all trades is a master of none but oftentimes better than a master of one" - That's why I mastered one language for the back-end and one for the front-end.

That said. C# and Java are general purpose languages that will allow you to write anything, and mastering just one of them will take a decade. For example I deal with C# and I'm currently learning .NET MAUI for mobile development, ASP .NET Core for API development and Blazor for front end. I just finished learning .NET Aspire for project orchestration and few testing frameworks. Don't even start me on latest feature of Roslyn compiler that allows live CodeGeneration! I love it so much!
I'm making a twitch chat game using typescript and tmi.js with no problems at all

Stick to what you know, and learn more from it as much as possible. Those skills you learned will always be transferable to the others, esp web apps. After that it will be ez pizzy when learning new technologies, plus it is bad to learn all technologies at once, it will overwhelm you.
